clinicalPearls: A rare skin disorder caused by the trichodysplasia spinulosa polyomavirus, which infects the inner root sheath cells of hair follicles
It occurs almost exclusively in immunocompromised patients, particularly solid-organ transplant recipients and those on intensive immunosuppression for haematological disease
The characteristic finding is numerous folliculocentric papules bearing keratinous spines, concentrated on the central face, especially the nose, eyebrows, and ears
Progressive involvement produces a thickened, spiny (leonine) facial appearance with loss of eyebrow and eyelash hair (madarosis) and alopecia
Histology shows dystrophic, enlarged hair follicles with abnormally proliferating inner root sheath cells containing trichohyaline granules and viral inclusions
Diagnosis is supported by skin biopsy, electron microscopy showing polyomavirus particles, and PCR detection of the trichodysplasia spinulosa polyomavirus
Management centres on reducing immunosuppression where possible, with topical antiviral or retinoid therapy reported to help; it can regress as immune function recovers
reference.pathophysiology: Trichodysplasia spinulosa is driven by active replication of a specific human polyomavirus that is probably acquired asymptomatically and remains latent in the skin of most people. When cell-mediated immunity is suppressed, as after organ transplantation, the virus reactivates and productively infects the inner root sheath cells of hair follicles. Uncontrolled viral replication drives abnormal proliferation and differentiation of these cells, with excessive accumulation of trichohyaline and formation of keratinous spines that protrude from distended, dystrophic follicles. The follicular architecture is disrupted, producing the spiny papules, facial thickening, and loss of hair characteristic of the condition. Because the disease depends on the failure of immune control, restoring immune function or reducing immunosuppression typically allows the follicular changes to regress.
additionalDifferentials: Multiple trichoepitheliomas or other adnexal tumours
Phrynoderma (vitamin A deficiency) and other follicular hyperkeratoses
Sarcoidosis or other granulomatous facial dermatoses
Drug-induced follicular eruptions in transplant recipients
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with histopathology of dystrophic follicles and abnormal inner root sheath proliferation
Electron microscopy demonstrating intranuclear polyomavirus particles
PCR for trichodysplasia spinulosa polyomavirus DNA from skin or spines
Review of the immunosuppressive regimen and degree of net immunosuppression
Assessment of underlying transplant or haematological condition
Dermatological examination to map the extent of facial and hair involvement
redFlags: Rapidly progressive facial disfigurement and hair loss
Extensive disease indicating heavy net immunosuppression
Diagnostic uncertainty raising concern for a follicular malignancy
Secondary bacterial infection of affected skin
reference.prognosis: The condition is disfiguring but not life-threatening, and it commonly improves or regresses when immunosuppression is reduced or immune function recovers; without such change it tends to persist and progress.
pitfalls: Mistaking the facial papules for keratosis pilaris or a benign follicular disorder and missing the diagnosis
Failing to link the eruption to the patient's immunosuppression
Not obtaining a biopsy or molecular testing to confirm the polyomavirus
Overlooking the potential for regression on reducing immunosuppression and pursuing unnecessary aggressive treatment
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
UpToDate: Trichodysplasia spinulosa and human polyomavirus skin disease
management: Reduce the net immunosuppression wherever transplant graft safety allows, as restoring cell-mediated immunity to control polyomavirus replication is the mainstay and often drives regression
Apply topical cidofovir to affected skin, or consider oral valganciclovir, as antiviral options reported to improve the folliculocentric spiny papules
Use topical retinoids or keratolytics and gentle physical removal of the keratinous spines for symptomatic and cosmetic improvement
Coordinate any change in immunosuppressive regimen with the transplant or haematology team, balancing viral control against the risk of graft rejection or disease relapse
Provide dermatological care with mapping and monitoring of facial and hair involvement, and surveillance for recurrence if immunosuppression is later intensified
Manage jointly through dermatology and the underlying transplant or haematology service, with counselling about the disfiguring but non-life-threatening nature of the condition
